paras: The killing of E. L. Little was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher by the city marshal of Conway, Arkansas, in April 1888. According to a dispatch from Conway, City Marshal John H. Howard shot Little after the preacher knocked him down with a can of peaches, and the story ran as a brief in papers from Texas to Rhode Island over the following three weeks. Other reports gave different names and causes for the quarrel.

Little was described as "a colored preacher" at Conway, and the Yorkville Enquirer called him the Rev. E. L. Little, "colored pastor of the African M. E. Church." The Enquirer traced the trouble to the marshal's arrest of Little's brother "for disturbance," while a Rock Island item said Little "had abused him for arrests he had made."

A dispatch dated Conway, April 13, and relayed through St. Louis, said the marshal had shot and killed Little "last night." In that account, the preacher had first knocked the marshal down with a can of peaches "for some unexplained affront." The Yorkville Enquirer, which dated the shooting to Thursday, said Little "undertook to remonstrate" with the marshal over his brother's arrest and "finally made an assault and was shot." In every version the marshal acted alone, and none mentions a crowd.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of the marshal, or any legal proceeding appears in the coverage, and no Arkansas paper's account was found.

The story reached readers almost entirely as a telegraphic or digest brief, first in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and the Rock Island Daily Argus on April 14. The Gazette headed it "Killed a Negro Preacher," and the Austin Weekly Statesman ran the same text as "Killed a Preacher." Papers in Kentucky and Ohio, among them the Hickman Courier, the Big Sandy News, the Hillsboro News-Herald, the Stark County Democrat and the Ohio Democrat, printed it under the headline "Fatal Can of Peaches."

A "South and West" digest column, carried in Rhode Island, West Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina between April 21 and May 2, reduced the event to one sentence that gave the motive as "some unknown reason." The Indiana State Sentinel's one-line notice gave no cause at all. All of these accounts presented the claim that Little struck or assaulted the marshal first without naming its source, and no paper offered editorial comment.

The marshal is John H. Howard in the wire report, "Harrell" in the Rock Island Argus and "John H. Harol" in the Yorkville Enquirer, the last probably a garbled Howard. The day also varies: the April 13 dispatch's "last night" and the Enquirer's "Thursday last" both point to April 12, while the Rock Island Argus, the Indiana State Sentinel and the Cambria Freeman said Friday. The cause appears as the can-of-peaches blow, as verbal abuse over arrests, or as an assault after a protest over Little's brother, and none of the reports identifies who supplied its version.

reader.title: Killing of E. L. Little
bases: Every report has a single officer, the city marshal of Conway, shooting Little, and none mentions a crowd or mob (A1, A2, A4).

Three differently worded reports, the St. Louis/Conway wire (A2), the Rock Island condensed item (A1) and the Yorkville Enquirer item (A4), agree that Conway's city marshal shot and killed the colored preacher Little, though they differ on the marshal's name, the day and the cause.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Conway dispatch under 'Fatal Can of Peaches' or 'Killed a Negro Preacher', giving only the marshal's side that the preacher struck first.
Digest columns reduced the killing to a single sentence among accidents and crimes, stating the motive as 'unknown'.
